summary: Proposes a format for a globally unique identifier for virtual private networks.

plainLanguage.summary: A unique ID number so every private network built over shared lines can be told apart.

questions: how is a vpn id formatted
subtitle: A globally unique name for a virtual private network: an organization ID plus a 4-octet index.

tldr.problem: Private IP networks can reuse the same addresses and can span several providers, so an IP address means nothing unless you know which VPN it belongs to, and there was no shared way to name a VPN.
tldr.mechanism: A VPN-ID is a 3-octet IEEE Organizationally Unique Identifier naming the VPN authority, followed by a 4-octet VPN index that picks one VPN run by that authority.
tldr.outcome: Any layer, provider or device can refer to the same VPN with the same value. The RFC defines only the format, not how the identifier is used.

today: RFC 2685 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It defines only the identifier format and leaves usage to other documents.

sections.title: Why VPNs Need an Identifier
sections.content:
A Virtual Private Network (VPN) emulates a private IP network over public or shared infrastructure. The RFC notes that many ways of providing VPN service were being discussed, and that the IP based VPN framework identifies four types: Virtual Leased Lines, Virtual Private Routed Networks, Virtual Private Dial Networks and Virtual Private LAN Segments.

Two points were agreed on by everyone. First, a VPN is private, so it may use a private address space that overlaps with another VPN or with the public Internet. Second, a VPN may span multiple Autonomous Systems or Service Providers.
sections.plainLanguage: Lots of private groups can use the same house numbers, and one group can live across many towns. So a house number alone is not enough to find the right house.

sections.title: The Purpose of a VPN-ID
sections.content:
Because addresses can overlap, an IP address only has meaning inside the VPN where it exists. The identifier tells you the "scope" of an address. Because several providers may serve one VPN, the RFC wants one identifier that works at any layer and at any location.

The VPN-ID might appear in a MIB, to assign an access interface to a VPN, or in a control or data packet, to show the scope of a private address. It can tie a packet to a VPN explicitly (for example in an encapsulation header as in RFC 2684) or implicitly (for example in an ATM signalling exchange). The same VPN can be identified at different layers, such as ATM and IP, and the same format and value should apply at both.

The identifier also names the VPN authority, which coordinates connectivity and services for the VPN. That may be the private network's administrator or its primary Service Provider. How the VPN-ID is used is beyond the scope of the memo.
sections.plainLanguage: The ID says which private group an address belongs to, and who is in charge of that group. It works the same way no matter which road, rail or air route the message takes.

sections.title: Format Requirements
sections.content:
The format has to meet three requirements:

  • Provide a globally unique identifier usable across multiple Service Providers.
  • Allow a VPN-ID that does not depend on IP, for use in layer 2 VPNs.
  • Identify the VPN authority within the identifier itself.

The format also must not assume anything about the shared networks, and must not prevent use of features of the shared network.
sections.plainLanguage: The name has to be one-of-a-kind everywhere, work even without IP addresses, and say who is in charge.

sections.title: The VPN Identifier Format
sections.content:
A global VPN identifier is a 3 octet VPN authority Organizationally Unique Identifier followed by a 4 octet VPN index. Each field is sent most significant octet first.

The OUI is an IEEE 802-1990 Organizationally Unique Identifier and identifies the VPN authority, the primary VPN administrator. That authority may be the company or organization the VPN belongs to, or a Service Provider that supplies the underlying infrastructure using its own or other providers' shared networks. The VPN index identifies one particular VPN serviced by that authority.
sections.plainLanguage: It is like a phone number with two parts: the first part says which company, and the second part says which of that company's private networks you mean.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The document defines the format without specifying usage. Tying capabilities to a VPN identifier means that standard security procedures are needed with any specified usage. The RFC warns that misconfiguring or deliberately forging a VPN identifier may cause different security breaches, including interconnecting different VPNs.
sections.plainLanguage: If someone writes the wrong name tag, or fakes one, two private groups might end up mixed together. So the tags must be handled carefully.

fields.name: VPN OUI
fields.desc: IEEE Organizationally Unique Identifier of the VPN authority (3 octets).

fields.name: VPN Index
fields.desc: Identifies a VPN serviced by that authority (4 octets).
